title: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
titleZh: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
author: albertzeyer
relevanceReason: 命中 6 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

comments.author: usernomdeguerre
comments.textRawHtml:
I feel like if the gap were so monumental that he could just point to a monument of it, rather than hand-waving at "the vertical professionals".

Alternative interpretation of the numbers; there's only a subset of productive work that LLM's are 'capable' of doing at this point. That is, work that's verifiable by a machine or doesn't require verification. Thus, the cleavage points are along that axis and-- naturally-- most human beings don't have that kind of work.

children.author: pjc50
children.textRawHtml:
> That is, work that's verifiable by a machine or doesn't require verification

That's where I'm at on the capabilities. LLMs have demolished software and mathematics because those have well-developed verification that's easier than doing the thing itself. Stuff that's more subjective they can produce good work, but with a significant error rate which makes it hard to let them loose on important client work without checking. Or rather, a number of companies are going through the cycle of trying that, having an expensive error, and reconsidering.

Or sometimes a company can simply pass the error cost onto consumers, who are gradually arming themselves with LLMs in response. We're going to see a productivity-sapping boom in disputes.

children.author: omnicognate
children.textRawHtml:
> demolished software and mathematics because those have well-developed verification that's easier than doing the thing itself

They are proving useful for the parts of those things that have that verification, but in neither case is that the whole of the field. In maths, for example, we have seen LLMs find answers to some interesting problems/conjectures, but haven't yet seen them pose any similarly interesting problems/conjectures themselves because the criteria for a "good conjecture" are unclear whereas the criteria for a resolution of an existing conjecture are usually supplied by the conjecture itself.

children.author: ndriscoll
children.textRawHtml:
Did anyone ask? i.e. did anyone with enough background to be able to judge whether a conjecture is "good" just point it at the repo of solved problems and ask it to formulate new conjectures based on the results/proofs? Or ask it to propose new structures to study? Or to identify a previously unknown general technique/tool that it had used in a proof?

It was asked to do a specific thing, and then its brain turned off/was reallocated to something else entirely (e.g. CRUD programming or answering celebrity trivia). It doesn't just idly think in its downtime. If we want it to do something else, we need to ask.

children.author: casey2
children.textRawHtml:
This is just moving the goalposts, yet again, all of mathematics has been hyper optimized on solving problem, proving theorems getting results and writing papers.

Only now that their job (the elites) has been automated was it really about explain results and theory building all this, despite those actions getting explicitly rejected from all the top journals (sans maybe math journals intended for a undergrad/high-school readership). People who weren't in the club and genuinely enjoy math are having the time of their life proving results. There is just a lot of groupthink and silent majority effects due to said elites running departments.

I use "theory-building" separately to Gowers since what he's talking about is field creation that solves tons of problems at once (Grothendieck, FTC, etc (I'll add AI itself here as a meta theory)) not making connections after the fact for the benefit of the lesser humans' understanding.

children.author: mizzao
children.textRawHtml:
The swarm-based HF hack, and the observation that 40-50% of the compute at AI labs goes into training the next generation of agents, doesn't count?

We're all over here using agents to code projects that used to take weeks and feeling pretty good about it, and they're using agents to build the next generation of frontier models — an order of magnitude more complex problem...

Whenever someone finds out how to apply this level of agentic sophistication to a problem that actually matters to consumers, then you'll have that monument that everyone can see.

children.author: TeMPOraL
children.textRawHtml:
It did a lot for consumers who dare to use it. It didn't do much for consumers who wait for middleman businesses to offer AI-based services, but that is not because of AI, but existing business model of SaaS.

The businesses pay for tokens and try to deliver their usual enshittified experience, and nothing interesting gets created, because it cannot - enshittification extinguishes all power of AI. Using AI to full extent, in contrast, obviates most need for the business in the first place. So they're all struggling to design an AI powered product, in a world where those very products are already becoming subsumed by AI.

So normies wait for middleware companies to get their shit together or (much more likely) finally die, while people with software experience and eagerness to use AI just don't subscribe, because their favorite LLM handles that work just fine.

children.author: koe123
children.textRawHtml:
With this stuff I immediately wish I was more economically literate. Bare with me. Let’s say one of these labs can use agents to replicate work otherwise done by humans. This proves that anyone with agents can eventually do this, unfortunately I don’t think its a moat like a platform (like facebook) provides, given that everyone is leapfrogging each-other constantly. Thus, it kind of becomes a commodity / low margin business?

Depending on the type of output, the value immediately (?) goes to the electricity cost of the LLMs and the cost of materials. So: more “efficient”, but without a big margin, right? So its cheaper for the workers that remain working, other workers are displaced, and capital owners now have a super slim margin business which can be instantly replicated at a place where material cost are lower (?).

Thus, it almost seems like “value add” by humans would in this simplified view be vastly diminished, and all that remains is resource wealth. Pop the materials in on one end and let the AI manufacture the product. Great news for the third world assuming the USA doesn't invade them.

Also, whose the consumer? Or are we going back to a strange medieval time where consumers are not of concern?

I don’t know what to think
